briefing.headline: The simulation predicts the policy would raise departures over the next 12 months from about 451 to about 1,226 out of 5,000 (+187%), roughly 775 extra leavers. Treat this as a strong warning sign rather than a precise forecast.
briefing.most_at_risk: Caregivers (+238%), long commuters (+228%) and mid-level staff (+211%) react worst because the rule adds hours of travel on top of school pickups, daycare and elder care, though even short-commute staff rise +150% because the badge tracking reads as distrust.
risks: Losing experienced mid-level people and caregivers, who are hardest to replace, while competitors in the same field still offer flexibility and recruiters are already calling.

Managers rise about as much as everyone else (+180%), and they are the ones asked to enforce the policy and review badge data; one engineering manager in the sample is 'already fielding recruiter emails.'
Requiring VP approval for exceptions feels 'insulting' to strong performers with care duties and could become a slow bottleneck, so many may start job hunting while they wait for an answer.
design_changes: Drop badge-swipe reviews with managers, or limit them to aggregate office-use data, since several voices with short commutes say their objection is 'the principle' of being tracked, not the travel.
Let individual managers grant exceptions under clear published criteria (caregiving, very long commutes) with a fast turnaround, instead of routing every case to a VP.
Let each team choose its own anchor days rather than imposing set company-wide days, and pair this with a longer, phased start than 90 days so caregivers can rearrange childcare and school runs.
briefing.confidence: medium. Every group moves sharply in the same direction and the voices give consistent reasons, so the direction is reliable. But the model rests on 48 voices (about two per group), and many respondents say they will 'look around' rather than definitely leave, so read 1,226 as a rough order of magnitude, and don't over-read small gaps such as women (+194%) versus men (+183%).

subgroup_checks.claim: Bigger rise for mid and senior managers
